statement: Resolution of U039: neither definition should be discarded, but they must be matched to different claims rather than averaged into one score. Retrieval-level claims - whether a retriever resolves version ambiguity - are scored by version identity, that is, whether the returned passage was in force at the target date, because that is the criterion legal analysis prescribes and what a legal benchmark encoding temporal validity measures; content scoring cannot detect contamination when successive versions share wording. End-to-end claims about user-visible harm are scored by answer accuracy restricted to the answer-differential stratum, because only there can a wrong version change the answer. Consequences: report the contamination rate, the screen pass rate and the conditional accuracy together, never a single aggregate; state in advance which metric adjudicates which claim so the dual reporting cannot be read as metric-shopping; and expect the two definitions to yield different magnitudes, with citation-validity failure more frequent than content failure. A residual definitional question arises for versions whose text is unchanged, where version-identity scoring would penalize retrieving an equivalent passage.
